notes:
Key findings:

1. **Critical gaps (high severity)**: Undo/redo command history (entire pattern missing), smart duplicate placement heuristics (no feature at all), and block edit latency optimizations (drag-session cache, debounce) are foundational Android features that iOS lacks entirely. These are substantial work.

2. **Moderate gaps**: Repair-with-AI hybrid (iOS doesn't distinguish fixed vs AI-assisted conflict repair), lack of dual UI buttons for Fix-schedule vs Repair-with-AI.

3. **Polish gaps**: Conflict arc rendering (visual feedback), live preview conflict validation (drag-time feedback), severity levels (BLOCKING vs WARNING).

4. **Database/performance**: iOS uses SwiftData with no visible WAL setting — may be fine (single-process) but should benchmark drag responsiveness on device before optimizing. Android's latency fix was driven by SQLCipher + Room, iOS has different perf profile.

5. **Shared logic**: resolveConflicts() algorithm is already ported to ChronosCore (iOS unit-tested). GapFillPlanner.propose() is ported as gapFill() helper but iOS GapFillSheet has a simplified local pack() instead of using ChronosCore.GapFill (readiness-aware break insertion is partly duplicated).

6. **Android-only features with no iOS analog**: None identified. All Day Dial features map to iOS native patterns.

7. **Undo scope note**: Android command history wraps both creation (CreateTimeBlockCommand) and moves/resizes from the timeline. iOS direct context.save() on every edit loses this audit trail. Command pattern belongs in ChronosCore (portable, testable) not UI layer.

8. **Conflict repair UX evolution**: Android recently split 'Fix schedule' (deterministic) from 'Repair with AI' (hybrid). iOS never had the deterministic button + AI fallback distinction; ConflictResolveSheet is only the deterministic version.

notes: ANDROID-ONLY FEATURES WITH NO iOS ANALOG: (1) ForegroundService lifecycle and onTaskRemoved recovery — iOS doesn't have a background-service model; app backgrounding + Live Activity is the replacement. (2) Per-phase EXTRA_TERMINAL mirroring to system (FocusExecutionStatus flags sent to FocusService via notifications) — iOS Live Activity just polls the in-app @Observable state. (3) Wear OS OngoingActivity mirroring for watch — iOS has WatchConnectivity; the sync already exists in PhoneWatchSync.publishFocusState() (FocusTimerModel line 304-317) and is feature-complete. SHARED DETERMINISTIC LOGIC: FocusPhasePlanner.plan() and focusMinutes() are already ported to FocusPhasePlan.swift and tested (FocusPhasePlanTests.swift green). iOS injectBreak() logic is also correct but UI is incomplete. RISK: Break injection and snapshot persistence are non-trivial changes. Snapshot persistence should go into ChronosCore or a new ChronosCore.Focus module with tests before shipping on iOS. TEST COVERAGE: ChronosCore tests (154 symbols green per memory) include FocusPhasePlanTests but NOT FocusTimerModel state machine tests; consider adding integration tests for inject/endBreak/phase boundary to ChronosCore (deterministic, not @main-dependent).

ANDROID-ONLY FEATURES (no iOS analog needed):
- Health Connect specifics (Android's HC API) → iOS uses HealthKit instead, already noted as separate work.

SHARED LOGIC TO PORT TO ChronosCore:
- journalParseBody / journalSerializeBody (body ↔ main note + sub-notes list)
- journalWordCount, journalAnsweredPromptKeys, journalMeterLabel (prompt scaffolding meter)
- journalIsOnlyPrompts, journalCanSave, journalCleanForSave (save validation)

- journalMoodByDate, journalMoodFor (mood enum lookups)
- journalStreak, journalStreakLabel (streak calculation)
- buildJournalInsightPrompt (AI prompt builder)

RISKS:
1. Sub-notes implementation: iOS currently has no sub-note model. Adding one requires updating JournalEntry schema + migration if deployed. Safest approach: store as serialized bullets in body string (matching Android's implementation), parse on display.
2. Multi-entry per day: iOS UI currently assumes one entry per day (todayEntry filter). Switching to multi-entry display requires redesigning history rendering.
3. HealthKit permission: request at app launch or in-sheet; handle denial gracefully (show Unavailable state).
4. Photo storage: iOS currently uses local file:// paths in photoUris. Ensure lifecycle is correct (temp files cleaned up if cancel, persisted on save).

MIGRATION PATH:
- Port deterministic helpers first (ChronosCore functions).
- Add time field + time picker next (localized effort).
- Add calendar grid (moderate complexity, but isolated to JournalView).
- Add sub-notes parsing + highlights editor (medium complexity, uses ChronosCore logic).
- Add multi-entry display + inline point adder (higher complexity, requires history redesign).
- Add HealthKit import (isolated feature, not blocking others).
- AI insights card (depends on Foundation models availability in target iOS version).

notes: Android-only HC features (incremental Changes-API, 6-hour periodic background sync via WorkManager, deletion-sweep via sweepDeletedRows) do not have direct iOS analogues because HealthKit lacks an equivalent Changes API. Readiness-aware planner logic (the 11:00 floor for DEPLETED mornings, adjusted break lengths) is at parity in GapFillSheet but missing in the single-task add-to-today flow. notes:
**Android-only features / no iOS sensible analog:** (1) Device calendar WRITE ACCESS (WRITE_CALENDAR permission) is Android-specific; iOS uses EKEventStore.requestFullAccessToEvents() which includes write. Export is implementable on iOS; just no existing UI. (2) WorkManager periodic scheduling is Android-specific; iOS uses BGTaskScheduler (already partially used for backup) — not a feature gap, just platform API difference. (3) CalendarContract Instances URI + ContentResolver queries are Android-specific; iOS uses EKEventStore predicateForEvents — different APIs, same functionality.

**Shared logic to port to ChronosCore once (use both Android + iOS):** (1) instanceUniqueId generation for recurring events — currently Android-only in CalendarEventRepositoryImpl, should move to ChronosCore as deterministic fn. (2) formatLastSyncedLabel relative time string — currently Android-only in RelativeTimeFormat.kt, candidate for ChronosCore. (3) Midnight-split logic for multi-day timed events — implement in ChronosCore as deterministic fn, reuse on iOS. (4) All-day event context marker creation — same. (5) Recurrence rule expansion + date range filtering — implement once in ChronosCore, both platforms call it.

**CRITICAL GAPS in order of severity:** (1) **No export to calendar** (HIGH) — blocks are view-only on iOS, can't be synced back to device calendar. Android users can 'export to calendar'; iOS users cannot. (2) **No background refresh** (HIGH) — iOS imported events never update unless user manually opens the app + taps overlay. Android user gets fresh events every 6h in the background. (3) **No provenance guards** (HIGH) — iOS doesn't prevent editing/deleting imported events, risking accidental corruption of the user's device calendar. (4) **No instance-unique IDs** (HIGH) — recurring calendar events would collide in iOS data model; no UI/data model issue YET because imports aren't actually written to disk, but will break when export is added. (5) **No sync status UI** (MEDIUM) — no 'last synced' feedback. (6) **No manual import UI** (MEDIUM) — Calendar overlay is read-only; no 'sync now' action.

**Risk notes:** (1) Calendar import/export is PERMISSION-GATED on both platforms; gate checks belong in the UI, not ChronosCore. (2) EventKit vs CalendarContract API surface differs significantly (recurrence rules, all-day semantics, availability enums) — need platform-specific adapters even though core logic is deterministic. (3) Recurring calendar events are a known complexity; iOS will need careful handling of EKRecurrenceRule expansion + edge-case all-day math. (4) All iOS changes require device/Mac testing (app target only builds on macOS/Xcode); assume the calendarEventID field will need migration when actual export writes begin.

**Also note:** The Android app's "AI app-function syncCalendarEvents" (mentioned in memory) is a device-only on-demand sync via app functions; iOS App Intents equivalent is NOT blocked by calendar parity — it's a separate system (iOS App Intents already exist but don't expose calendar sync yet). Calendar sync parity is about the DATA/UI layer, not AI intents.

Android-only features requiring iOS analogs or noting as N/A: (1) Screen-time nudges on a dedicated IMPORTANCE_LOW channel — iOS lacks a built-in screen-time API, so this is delegated to App Intents / Shortcuts or a background task. iOS ChronosSettings has screenTimeEnabled but no notification channel. Leave as-is for now (not a parity blocking issue). (2) CRITICAL_CHANNEL_ID for medication/urgent tasks — iOS uses interruptionLevel .timeSensitive instead. (3) Notification permissions check (canPostPromotedNotifications) — iOS doesn't expose this; assume the system decides based on user settings. (4) ReminderNotificationGroups.refreshSummary() with InboxStyle summary — iOS threads group notifications automatically; no equivalent maintenance call needed. (5) Wear OS live updates (OngoingActivity per-phase mirroring) — iOS equivalent is watchOS ActivityKit, which is separate from phone notifications.

Shared deterministic logic: QuietHours.swift is already in ChronosCore (buildable/testable). Notification action handling (dose-taken → supply-check) should also be ported to ChronosCore as a pure function so both app and tests can verify refill-warning logic deterministically. Currently MedicationActionReceiver.kt has the logic; equivalent should live in ChronosCore or a shared ViewModel in iOS.

Risks: (1) Refill-soon posting from the 'Taken' action could cause badge spam if the supply drops gradually. Android uses AlarmDeliveryCoordinator.deliverLowSupplyWarning() which is explicit and gated. iOS should do the same — post refill warning ONLY once per refill cycle (store a flag in UserDefaults). (2) Current-block ActivityKit may collide with focus Live Activity if both fire at once — needs careful gating in onFocusStarted()/onFocusEnded(). (3) Deep-link routing with blockId requires testing on device to ensure the FocusView picker/auto-start integrates correctly.

notes:
**Android-only pattern note:** InteropProvider (content-provider-based peer verification with signature-pinned trust) has no exact iOS equivalent. iOS cross-app sharing uses App Groups (entitlement-based) rather than content providers + signing certs. DevTime/Meridian on iOS would need App Groups coordination and a separate native SecureEnclave flow — not addressed in this scope. The medication-sharing consent toggle can live on both platforms independently (user grants it in each app separately).

**Shared deterministic logic:** The privacy preferences schema (redaction toggles, medication sharing opt-in, cloud sync flag, watch sync status) should be ported to ChronosCore once finalized on iOS, so both app + widgets/intents see consistent state (mirrors Android's DataStore pattern). WearLinkStatus and WearLinkStatusProvider are pure domain—ready for ChronosCore now.

**Collapsible section persistence:** Android uses DataStore (UI-settings namespace); iOS uses UserDefaults App-Group. The key naming pattern is identical (privacy.sectionName.expanded), so once iOS ChronosCore is mature, a shared Settings contract could codegen defaults for both.

**Risk:** The watch sync status feature relies on ChronosSettings recording the last-push timestamp—if PhoneWatchSync.pushSnapshot() is called elsewhere and doesn't update the timestamp, the UI will show stale data. Requires disciplined timestamp writes in all sync paths.

**Testing:** 6 gaps affect user-visible privacy controls and interop readiness. Gaps 1 & 2 (Meridian + collapsibles) are prerequisites for App-Group / Watch Connectivity syncing to be user-discoverable. Gap 3 is low-risk cosmetic. Gaps 4 & 5 (watch/iCloud status display + app permissions breakdown) are UX polish but should be done before launch to match Android parity on sync visibility.

gaps.iosState: No app-identity verification; no bundle-ID pinning; no way to confirm DevTime is the real app vs a spoofing app using a custom URL scheme
gaps.work: 1) Add bundle identifier validation: when checking if DevTime is installed, verify via URL scheme opening or App Groups (if DevTime writes to shared container, confirm it's readable by a bundle ID check); 2) Add a simple pin: store expected DevTime bundle ID (com.Meridian.VBCR) in InteropContract; 3) When querying DevTime data via custom URL scheme, confirm DevTime's Team ID (Apple Developer account ID, visible in entitlements/bundle signature) matches expected—though this is harder on iOS without private APIs; 4) For App Groups approach, trust is implicit (DevTime must grant the shared group entitlement + iOS enforces team-based access); document the trust model in a privacy/security comment
gaps.iosApproach: iOS entitlements + team-based sandbox provide the security boundary (no explicit certificate pinning API); rely on App Group access control + document DevTime team ID requirement; for URL scheme, validate bundle ID in response data

gaps.iosState: No Settings UI component showing if DevTime is installed or linked; no visual feedback on interop status; no disclosure dialog asking user to consent; no medication-sharing toggle for interop

gaps.title: No export of ChronosFlow tasks to DevTime (iOS missing InteropProvider server-side)
gaps.androidBehavior: InteropProvider.kt exposes read-only provider at content://${applicationId}.share/tasks, /events, /habits, /medications, /goals; only serves rows where origin IS NULL (self-authored, not re-shared imports); gated by consent + cert verification; allows DevTime to pull ChronosFlow's data
gaps.iosState: iOS has no mechanism to expose its tasks/habits/medications to DevTime; iOS is read-only (imports from DevTime, does not publish); asymmetric data flow
gaps.work: OPTIONAL for iOS (may be lower priority than ingestion): Implement task/habit/medication export via: 1) App Group shared UserDefaults/JSON file updated whenever local data changes (simpler but polling-heavy); 2) Custom URL scheme handler (devtime://query?type=tasks) that returns JSON response (requires DevTime to call ChronosFlow, not push); 3) Note: iOS does not have ContentProvider, so the Android provider model does not map 1:1; the simpler MVP is unidirectional (DevTime → ChronosFlow import only)
gaps.iosApproach: For MVP: unidirectional import only (covered by sync worker + privacy toggle); if bidirectional needed later: custom URL scheme handler in AppDelegate/SceneDelegate or shared App Group container with change notifications

gaps.title: No deduplication of DevTime imports on iOS (iOS missing InteropSyncManager collapse logic)
gaps.androidBehavior: InteropSyncManager.kt collapses near-identical upstream rows (same trimmed/lowercased title + due time) into one so accidental duplicates in DevTime don't multiply on import (lines 55–57); tracks priorImportedIds and deletes stale rows in a transaction (lines 59–89); upserts use deterministic ID built from origin + externalId (line 66: id = 'interop:com.Meridian.VBCR:${externalId}')
gaps.iosState: No dedup logic when mirroring tasks; no tracking of imported-vs-self-authored tasks; no transaction-like batch operation to clean up stale imports
gaps.work: In InteropSync implementation: 1) Add a TaskImport model with origin field (set to 'com.Meridian.VBCR'); 2) When syncing, build deterministic ID as 'interop:com.Meridian.VBCR:\(externalId)'; 3) Collapse duplicates via distinctBy { (title.trim().lowercased(), dueDate) }; 4) Delete TaskItem records where origin == 'com.Meridian.VBCR' and id NOT IN keepIds (batch delete in a modelContext transaction); 5) Store externalId on each imported TaskItem for future dedup
gaps.iosApproach: SwiftData transactions via modelContext.delete() in batch; deterministic ID generation; FilteredSet/Set dedupe logic in Swift

gaps.title: No max-import limit on DevTime task count (iOS missing MAX_INTEROP_TASKS cap)
gaps.androidBehavior: InteropSyncManager.kt caps imports at 500 tasks (MAX_INTEROP_TASKS=500, line 133); logs warning if DevTime has more (lines 52–54); prevents pathological cases where DevTime has thousands of tasks and crashes iOS memory
gaps.iosState: No upper limit on imported task count; potential for DoS if DevTime returns huge datasets
gaps.work: In InteropSync.syncFromPeer(), after fetching DevTime tasks, if count > 500: log warning, take first 500, discard remainder
gaps.iosApproach: Simple array slice via Swift's Array(tasks.prefix(500))

gaps.title: No Android-like manifest/entitlements setup for inter-app access (iOS info.plist/entitlements missing Meridian reference)
gaps.androidBehavior: app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml declares <queries> package for com.Meridian.VBCR (allows ChronosFlow to detect install); <provider> declares the shared authority (allows DevTime to query); runtime permissions not needed (signature-level gating via PeerVerifier)
gaps.iosState: Info.plist has no mention of DevTime/Meridian or custom URL schemes for interop; ChronosFlow.entitlements has app group but no reference to companion-app scheme/identifier
gaps.work: 1) Add to Info.plist: LSApplicationQueriesSchemes array including 'devtime' or custom scheme (needed to call UIApplication.canOpenURL()); 2) Add to ChronosFlow.entitlements: com.apple.security.application-groups = ['group.com.chronosflow.shared', 'group.com.devtime.shared'] IF DevTime uses a separate app group; 3) Document the expected DevTime bundle ID and Team ID in a comment (for future verification logic)
gaps.iosApproach: Standard Info.plist + entitlements XML configuration; LSApplicationQueriesSchemes for URL scheme discovery; app-group entitlements for shared container access

notes: Android-only features with no direct iOS analog: ContentProvider-based inter-app querying is Android-specific; iOS uses App Groups + URL schemes. The Android WorkManager pattern maps to iOS BGTaskScheduler + URLSession background fetch. Signature-certificate pinning (PeerVerifier) is Android-specific; iOS relies on code-signing entitlements + team-based sandbox. ChronosFlow on iOS should prioritize the sync-worker + import pipeline (critical path) before bidirectional export (nice-to-have). Shared deterministic logic (dedup, reminder scheduling, max-import cap) should ideally move into ChronosCore as testable Swift functions once devised, so both Android and iOS benefit from the same algorithms—though current Android versions are already tested in InteropSyncWorkerDedupTest.kt and InteropSyncManagerTests (inferred from memory notes). Consider that iOS users can only import FROM DevTime (read-only), not publish TO it, until custom URL scheme handlers or App Group file-based export is added. Release cert pinning (DevTime's SHA-256) is a TODO in Android (DEVTIME_RELEASE_CERT_SHA256 = "") and should be coordinated cross-platform before shipping.
